note: A consensus checklist of 27 reporting items, which an audit can use directly to test whether an early clinical study was adequately reported.
title: Reporting guideline for the early stage clinical evaluation of decision support systems driven by artificial intelligence: DECIDE-AI

reading.body:
DECIDE-AI is a 27-item consensus checklist for reporting early clinical studies of AI decision support, built because those reports were leaving out details readers needed.

The checklist splits into 17 AI-focused items, expanded into 28 subitems, and 10 general items. It was produced through a modified Delphi process: two rounds of expert input from 20 predefined stakeholder groups, 123 experts in the first round and 138 in the second, with 16 people at a virtual consensus meeting and 16 in a qualitative evaluation. Each item carries an Explanation and Elaboration paragraph, so the checklist is meant to be applied, not just cited.

The gap it addresses is specific to AI. Small early clinical studies are where a model's real-world performance, safety, and clinician interaction are supposed to be checked, and the authors' position is that reporting of these studies has been weak. A checklist does not make a model better. It makes the evidence about the model legible, which is the precondition for anyone deciding whether a larger trial or wider adoption is warranted.

What the data does not contain is any measure of whether the guideline worked. There is no count of studies that adopted it, no before-and-after comparison of reporting quality, and no clinical outcome. The 722 citations indicate the paper is widely referenced, but citation counts do not establish that reporting improved. The data also says nothing about compute, data centers, or power, so no claim about infrastructure can be drawn from it.

explain_beginner: Many AI tools that help doctors make decisions look promising in computer tests, but few have been shown to improve patient care. Small early clinical studies are meant to check how these tools work in real settings, whether they are safe, and how people use them. The authors found that reports of such studies often leave out important details. So they worked with many experts to agree on a checklist for what these studies should report. The checklist has 17 AI-related items, split into 28 smaller points, plus 10 general items. This matters because clearer reports help others judge and repeat the work.
explain_business: Many AI tools for clinical decisions perform well in early testing, but few have proven patient benefit. Small early clinical studies are where safety, real performance, and how clinicians interact with them should be checked, yet their reporting has been weak. DECIDE-AI gives executives a consensus checklist of 27 reporting items, covering AI-focused and general concerns, with guidance for each. In practice, it can be used to judge whether an early study is complete enough to trust, to appraise the evidence, and to decide whether to support larger trials or wider adoption. It informs decisions about investment, procurement, and oversight.
explain_practitioner: The authors tackled weak reporting in small clinical studies of AI decision support. They used a modified Delphi exercise with two rounds to gather expert views from 20 predefined stakeholder groups. Participation included 123 experts in round one, 138 in round two, 16 at a virtual consensus meeting, and 16 in a qualitative evaluation. The final DECIDE-AI guideline has 17 items focused on AI, divided into 28 subitems, and 10 general items. Each item comes with an Explanation and Elaboration paragraph. This consensus checklist is meant to help researchers describe early clinical evaluations clearly, so others can judge the studies and reproduce their findings.
